subject: anatomy
title: Posterior Thigh: Hamstrings, Profunda Femoris, and Cruciate Anastomosis

steps.tx: The posterior compartment of the thigh contains the **hamstring muscles**, comprising semimembranosus, semitendinosus, the long head of biceps femoris, and the ischial part of adductor magnus. To qualify as a true hamstring, a muscle must arise from the ischial tuberosity, span both hip and knee joints, and receive tibial nerve innervation.
steps.say: The posterior thigh contains the hamstring muscles: semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris long head, and ischial adductor magnus. True hamstrings arise from the ischial tuberosity, span two joints, and receive tibial nerve innervation.

steps.tx: The short head of the biceps femoris is not a morphological hamstring. It arises from the lateral lip of the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur, crosses only the knee joint, and is innervated by the **common peroneal nerve**. The combined biceps tendon inserts onto the head of the fibula, split by the fibular collateral ligament.
steps.say: The short head of biceps femoris is not a true hamstring because it originates from the femur and crosses only the knee. It receives innervation from the common peroneal nerve and inserts with the long head onto the fibular head.

steps.tx: Muscular branches of the **profunda femoris artery** (deep artery of the thigh) provide the chief arterial supply to all compartments of the thigh. Arising from the lateral aspect of the femoral artery approximately 3.5 centimetres distal to the inguinal ligament, it descends behind the adductor longus close to the femur.
steps.say: The profunda femoris artery is the main arterial trunk supplying the thigh musculature. Originating three and a half centimeters below the inguinal ligament, it descends behind adductor longus close to the femur.

vis.caption: Femoropopliteal arterial anatomy showing profunda femoris branching and collateral pathways. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Near its origin, the profunda femoris gives off the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries. Distally, it terminates by giving off **four perforating arteries** that pierce the aponeurosis of adductor magnus near the linea aspera, forming a longitudinal anastomotic arterial chain supplying the posterior hamstring compartment.
steps.say: Near its root, the profunda gives off circumflex femoral arteries before terminating as four perforators. These perforating vessels pierce adductor magnus along the linea aspera, forming a vital collateral chain in the hamstrings.

steps.tx: At the level of the lesser trochanter, an essential collateral vascular crossway is formed known as the **cruciate anastomosis**. This anastomosis links branches of the internal iliac artery with branches of the external iliac and femoral systems, maintaining lower limb perfusion if the superficial femoral or external iliac artery is occluded.
steps.say: At the lesser trochanter, the cruciate anastomosis bridges the internal and external iliac systems. This collateral network maintains perfusion to the lower extremity if the femoral or external iliac artery becomes blocked.

steps.tx: The trochanteric anastomosis complements the cruciate network, situated in the trochanteric fossa of the femur. Receiving ascending branches from medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries and the superior gluteal artery, it is the primary distributor of retinacular branches supplying the **femoral head**.
steps.say: The trochanteric anastomosis lies in the trochanteric fossa, fed by ascending circumflex femoral branches and the superior gluteal artery. It supplies the essential retinacular vessels that nourish the femoral head.

vis.alt: Trochanteric anastomosis and retinacular branches to the femoral head
vis.caption: Trochanteric arterial anastomosis contributing ascending branches to the femoral head. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Distally, the femoral vessels pass through the **adductor hiatus**, a tendinous gap in the aponeurotic insertion of adductor magnus. Traversing this hiatus transitions the femoral artery and vein from the anterior compartment into the popliteal fossa, where they become renamed the popliteal artery and popliteal vein.
steps.say: Distally, femoral vessels pass through the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus. Crossing this opening transitions the vessels into the popliteal fossa, where they are designated the popliteal artery and vein.

steps.tx: Acute hamstring strain frequently affects the musculotendinous junction during the terminal swing phase of high-speed sprinting, when the muscles undergo forceful eccentric contraction to decelerate knee extension. Avulsion fractures of the **ischial tuberosity** occur in adolescent sprinters when the common hamstring tendon violently pulls away its secondary ossification centre.
steps.say: Hamstring tears frequently occur during sprinting when the muscle eccentrically decelerates knee extension. In adolescent athletes, violent contraction can avulse the secondary ossification center of the ischial tuberosity.
